t: Inherited-looking elegance: logo-free, beautifully made, never in a hurry.
d: Old Money dresses like the clothes were bought decades ago and cared for ever since. Quality fabrics, neutral colours and conservative cuts do the talking; logos, trends and visible effort are avoided. It overlaps with what the internet calls quiet luxury.
o: Rooted in East Coast and European upper-class dressing of the mid-20th century (sailing, equestrian and country-club wardrobes), revived online from 2022 by TV costume design and the quiet-luxury conversation.
k: Simple gold jewellery or a heritage watch
do: Buy fewer, better pieces and tailor them
Keep colours within navy, camel, cream, grey and deep greens
Look after shoes and knitwear visibly well
dont: Wear visible logos or monograms everywhere
st: Swap one logo item for a plain, well-made equivalent
Get your best trousers and blazer altered to fit
Build outfits around one neutral base: navy or camel
w: Anyone who wants a polished, trend-proof wardrobe that reads expensive without saying so.
b: Second-hand cashmere and vintage leather goods give the look at a fraction of the price.

t: Fewer pieces, cleaner lines, more outfits.
d: Minimalist fashion strips an outfit to clean silhouettes, a tight palette and excellent fit. A small wardrobe of interchangeable basics replaces trend pieces, so every item works with almost every other.
o: Grew from 1990s designers who rejected 80s excess, and from the capsule-wardrobe idea popularised in the 1970s and revived by bloggers in the 2010s.
do: Pick a 3–4 colour palette and stick to it
Prioritise fit and fabric over details
dont: Buy one-off statement pieces that match nothing
Confuse minimal with sloppy: pressed and tailored matters
st: List your 10 most-worn items and find the common thread
Remove anything that clashes with your palette
Fill gaps with neutral basics only
w: People who want getting dressed to take two minutes and still look put-together.
b: Spend on outerwear and shoes; buy tees and knits mid-range and replace yearly.

t: The pieces that have worked for 70 years and will work for 70 more.
d: Classic style relies on garments whose shapes barely change: trench coats, white shirts, straight jeans, little black dresses and tailored jackets. It is less about a mood and more about reliability: everything fits, everything matches.
o: Built from mid-century wardrobe staples codified by designers and fashion editors as investment pieces.
k: Little black dress or navy suit
do: Invest in tailoring once a year
Use one accent colour, such as red, sparingly
dont: Mix too many eras in one outfit
st: Get a trench, a white shirt and dark jeans that fit perfectly
Add one blazer in navy or black
w: Professionals and anyone who wants their wardrobe to age well.
b: Classic pieces resell well, so buying quality second-hand is low-risk.

t: Sneaker culture, graphic layers and limited drops.
d: Streetwear mixes skate, hip-hop and sportswear codes into oversized, graphic-led outfits. Sneakers anchor the look and scarcity (drops, collaborations) drives desire.
o: Emerged from 1980s–90s surf, skate and hip-hop scenes in California, New York and Tokyo, then merged with luxury fashion in the 2010s.
do: Build around one hero pair of sneakers
Play with proportion: oversized top, relaxed bottom
dont: Wear head-to-toe logos from different brands
Let everything be the same oversized fit with no shape
st: Add a heavyweight hoodie in a neutral
Layer a technical or varsity jacket
w: Casual dressers who love sneakers, music and youth culture.
b: Quality blanks and vintage sportswear look as good as hyped drops.

t: Free-spirited layers, prints and natural textures.
d: Boho fashion layers flowing silhouettes, earthy prints and handcrafted accessories. It feels relaxed, romantic and well-travelled, mixing vintage, folk and festival references.
o: Draws on 19th-century artistic bohemians and 1960s–70s counterculture, revived by festival fashion in the 2000s.
do: Mix prints that share a colour
Keep one element fitted for balance
dont: Pile on every accessory at once
st: Start with a flowing midi or maxi dress
Add a suede or denim layer
Finish with one artisanal piece of jewellery
w: Creative, outdoorsy people who like comfort with personality.
b: Vintage and second-hand shops are full of boho staples.

t: Tweed, books and candlelit libraries.
d: Dark Academia borrows the uniform of an old university: tweed, wool, plaid and loafers in deep, moody colours. It is as much about mood (studying, poetry, old buildings) as about clothes.
o: Took shape online around 2015 on Tumblr and later TikTok, inspired by campus novels and films set at old universities.
do: Keep the palette dark and warm
Add vintage glasses or a pocket watch for character
dont: Go full costume with capes and quills
st: Pair it with a dark turtleneck
w: Bookish people, students and anyone who loves autumn year-round.
b: Charity shops are the best source for authentic tweed and wool.

t: Dark Academia's sunnier sibling: linen, cream and poetry in the park.
d: Light Academia keeps the scholarly references but swaps the moody palette for cream, beige and soft brown. Linen, cotton and loose knits make it airy and optimistic.
o: Grew online alongside Dark Academia from around 2019 as a softer, spring-and-summer counterpart.
k: Pleated cream trousers or midi skirt
do: Keep the palette light and warm
Accessorise with books and simple jewellery
dont: Mix in black or harsh contrast
st: Swap one dark knit for a cream cardigan
w: Romantic, curious types who like a soft, literary look.
b: Linen is pricey new; vintage linen shirts are plentiful.

t: Pastoral romance: florals, puff sleeves and homemade bread.
d: Cottagecore idealises a slow countryside life. Prairie dresses, florals, aprons and natural fabrics evoke gardens, baking and handcraft.
o: Named online around 2018 and boomed in 2020 as people sought comfort and nature during lockdowns.
dont: Make every piece frilly at once
w: Romantics, gardeners and makers.
b: Sew or upcycle: cottagecore rewards handmade.

t: Low-rise, baby tees and shiny everything: the 2000s, remixed.
d: Y2K revives turn-of-the-millennium fashion: low-rise jeans, baby tees, butterfly clips, tinted sunglasses and metallics. It is playful, a little kitsch and pop-culture driven.
o: Originally late-1990s to mid-2000s pop and tech optimism; revived by Gen Z on social media from around 2020.
do: Pick one or two 2000s signatures per outfit
dont: Recreate a full 2003 look head to toe
st: Add a baby tee to your usual jeans
w: Trend-lovers and anyone with a playful streak.
b: Thrift stores still hold real 2000s pieces.

t: Flannel, combat boots and a deliberate lack of polish.
d: Grunge is anti-fashion: worn flannel, ripped denim, band tees and boots layered with an undone attitude. The point is comfort and rebellion rather than perfection.
o: Came out of the Seattle music scene of the late 1980s and early 1990s and was famously put on a runway in 1993.
do: Mix feminine slip dresses with boots
st: Throw a flannel over a dark tee
w: Music fans and people who hate dressing up.
b: The most authentic grunge pieces are second-hand.

t: Polos, chinos and boat shoes: campus-classic and crisp.
d: Preppy style comes from American prep schools and Ivy League campuses: polos, Oxford shirts, chinos, cable knits and blazers in clean, cheerful colours. It is tidy, sporty and optimistic.
o: Codified in mid-20th-century US East Coast universities and spread worldwide by catalogues and the 1980 'Official Preppy Handbook'.
do: Use one bright colour with navy or khaki
st: Buy an Oxford shirt and chinos
w: Sporty, sociable types who like a fresh, polished look.
b: Preppy basics are cheap and plentiful second-hand.

t: Linen, sea air and a farmers'-market tote.
d: Coastal Grandmother is breezy, comfortable luxury: white linen, cashmere throws, striped tops and wide-brim hats, as if you live in a beach house and cook every evening.
o: Named on TikTok in 2022, inspired by the wardrobes of romantic-comedy heroines in seaside homes.
do: Keep it light, neutral and relaxed
Add a straw or woven accessory
st: Add espadrilles and a straw hat
w: Anyone who wants holiday-level ease every day.
b: Linen softens with age, so worn second-hand linen is a win.

t: Functional minimalism with a playful Copenhagen twist.
d: Scandi style combines practical, high-quality basics with relaxed silhouettes and occasional bold colour or print. It is designed for bikes, rain and real life, yet always looks considered.
o: Associated with Danish and Swedish brands and the street style around Copenhagen Fashion Week from the 2010s.
do: Add one playful colour or print
dont: Wear impractical heels for city days
st: Wear it with straight jeans and a knit
w: Practical people who still want to look current.
b: Scandi brands resell strongly second-hand, so prices stay fair.

t: Gym-ready pieces styled for everything else.
d: Athleisure wears performance fabrics outside the gym: leggings, joggers, technical layers and sneakers styled with polished pieces like blazers or long coats.
o: Rose through the 2010s as stretch activewear became comfortable and stylish enough for daily wear.
k: Long wool coat to dress it up
do: Add one tailored piece for contrast
dont: Wear faded or stretched gym kit out
w: Busy, active people who live in comfortable clothes.
b: Mid-range activewear performs well; pay more only for fit.

t: Technical outdoor gear worn in the city.
d: Gorpcore turns hiking and climbing gear into street style: fleeces, shell jackets, trail shoes and utility pants in earthy or bright technical colours.
o: The name comes from 'good ol' raisins and peanuts' trail mix; it emerged in fashion writing around 2017.
do: Mix one bright technical piece with neutrals
Choose gear you would really use
dont: Wear every logo from every outdoor brand
Forget the outfit still needs shape
w: Outdoor lovers and practical dressers.
b: Outlet and second-hand outdoor gear is durable and cheap.

t: Professional without the full suit.
d: Business casual blends tailored pieces with relaxed ones: trousers or skirts with knitwear, shirts or blouses, and smart shoes. It signals competence while staying comfortable for long days.
o: Spread through US offices in the 1990s as 'casual Friday' grew into everyday policy.
do: Choose neutral bases with one colour
Match the formality of your workplace
dont: Wear athletic sneakers unless your office allows it
st: Buy two pairs of well-fitting trousers
w: Office workers and anyone with client meetings.
b: A tailor turns budget trousers into expensive-looking ones.

t: Slick bun, glowing skin, gold hoops, effortless basics.
d: The Clean Girl aesthetic is about looking fresh and put-together with minimal effort: slicked-back hair, dewy skin, simple gold jewellery and neutral, fitted basics.
o: Went viral on TikTok around 2022, drawing on long-standing beauty looks; it has been critiqued for ignoring the communities that originated some of its signatures.
st: Wear a neutral fitted top with relaxed trousers
w: People who like a low-maintenance, polished look.
b: Grooming matters more than price tags here.

t: Bows, lace and pale pink with a knowing wink.
d: Coquette leans into hyper-feminine details: ribbons, lace, ballet flats, pearls and soft pastels. It is romantic, girlish and nostalgic, often mixing vintage lingerie-inspired pieces with everyday basics.
o: Grew on Tumblr in the 2010s and peaked on TikTok around 2023–2024 alongside balletcore.
do: Use one or two romantic details per look
dont: Wear it in settings that need formal attire
st: Tie a ribbon in your hair
w: Romantics who love femininity and vintage details.
b: Ribbons and lace trims transform cheap basics.

t: Cowboy boots, denim and turquoise, styled for the city.
d: Western style takes ranch and rodeo staples (boots, denim, fringe, big buckles and turquoise) and wears them as fashion. It ranges from rugged to glamorous.
o: Rooted in 19th-century American ranch wear, repeatedly revived by music and film, including a major comeback from 2023.
do: Pick one western hero piece per look
dont: Wear a full costume with hat, chaps and spurs
st: Add cowboy boots to jeans and a tee
w: Adventurous dressers who like a rugged edge.
b: Vintage boots are often better made than new fast-fashion versions.

t: Black, waterproof, strapped and ready for the city of the future.
d: Techwear combines performance fabrics with utilitarian design: waterproof shells, cargo pants with straps and buckles, and a mostly black palette. Function and a futuristic look matter equally.
o: Developed from technical outerwear and Japanese and German urban labels in the 2000s–2010s.
w: Urban commuters, cyclists and sci-fi fans.
b: Military surplus offers functional pieces cheaply.

t: Effortless, a little undone and always flattering.
d: Parisian chic is a few perfect basics worn with confidence: a Breton top, straight jeans, a trench, ballet flats and red lipstick. It looks unplanned but relies on fit and restraint.
o: A long-running fashion ideal built around Parisian women, popularised by mid-century style icons and later by books and influencers.
st: Wear a Breton top with straight jeans
w: Anyone who wants to look chic without trying hard.
b: A good trench and jeans cover most of the look.

t: Faux fur, leopard print, gold and unapologetic glamour.
d: The Mob Wife aesthetic is loud luxury: big faux-fur coats, animal print, black leather, oversized sunglasses and chunky gold. It is the opposite of quiet luxury.
o: Went viral on TikTok in early 2024, inspired by glamorous characters in crime films and TV.
dont: Buy real fur unless second-hand and ethical to you
st: Add a faux-fur coat over black basics
w: Bold dressers who enjoy glamour and drama.
b: Second-hand faux fur and costume gold give maximum impact for little.

t: Tailored menswear worn with studied nonchalance.
d: Sprezzatura is the Italian art of making great tailoring look effortless: soft jackets, open collars, rolled sleeves and a slightly imperfect tie. It rewards fit, texture and confidence.
o: The word comes from a 1528 Italian book on courtly manners; in menswear it became shorthand for Neapolitan and Florentine style, especially around the Pitti Uomo trade fair.
st: Pair with pleated trousers and an open-collar shirt
w: Men who want tailored style that feels relaxed.
b: Unstructured jackets are easy to find second-hand and alter.
